'''Adriaan "Ad" Bax''' (born 1956) is a Dutch-American molecular biophysicist who is a Distinguished Investigator at the [[National Institutes of Health]]. He is the Chief of the Section on Biophysical NMR Spectroscopy in the Laboratory of Chemical Physics at the [[National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases]]. He is known for his work on the methodology of [[protein nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy|biomolecular NMR spectroscopy]]. He is a corresponding member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]], a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and a Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Adriaan Bax, Ph.D., NIH Distinguished Investigator - NIDDK |url=https://www.niddk.nih.gov/about-niddk/staff-directory/biography/bax-adriaan |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Biography==
Bax was born in the Netherlands. He studied at [[Delft University of Technology]] where he got his [[engineer's degree]] (Ir. degree) in 1978 and his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] degree in Applied Physics in 1981, after spending considerable time working with [[Ray Freeman]] at [[University of Oxford|Oxford University]]. He continued as a [[postdoctoral research|postdoc]] with Gary Maciel in the National Solid-State facility at [[Colorado State University]], before joining the NIH's Laboratory of Chemical Physics in 1983. In 1994 he became Correspondent of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/3840 |title=A. Bax |publisher=[[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]] |access-date=18 July 2015 |archive-date=21 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721201905/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/correspondents/3840 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  In 2002 he was elected a Member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in the section on [[List of members of the National Academy of Sciences (Biophysics and computational biology)|Biophysics and computational biology]] and a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Adriaan Bax – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/adriaan-bax-fsuqip/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=nasonline.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|access-date=May 28, 2011}}</ref> Bax was awarded the 2018 [[NAS Award for Scientific Reviewing]] in structural biology and the 2018 [[Welch Award in Chemistry]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Welch Award in Chemistry |url=http://www.welch1.org/awards/welch-award-in-chemistry |website=www.welch1.org}}</ref> He was elected a Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]] in 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Outstanding scientists elected as Fellows of the Royal Society {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2024/05/new-fellows-2024/ |access-date=2024-05-19 |website=royalsociety.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Work in NMR spectroscopy==

Bax works in the field of biomolecular NMR spectroscopy and has been a leader in the development of what have become today's standard methods in the field.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Welch Foundation is honored to announce the 2018 Robert A. Welch… |url=https://welch1.org/news-reports/news/the-welch-foundation-is-honored-to-announce-the-2018-robert-a-welch-award-in-chemistry-recipient |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=Welch}}</ref> He collaborated extensively with fellow NIH scientists [[Marius Clore]], [[:de:Angela_Gronenborn|Angela Gronenborn]] and [[Dennis Torchia]] in the development of multidimensional [[protein NMR]].<ref name=clore>{{cite book|last1=Clore|first1=Marius G|title=Encyclopedia of Magnetic Resonance|date=2011|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]]|isbn=9780470034590|chapter-url=http://spin.niddk.nih.gov/clore/Pub/pdf/432.pdf|chapter=Adventures in Biomolecular NMR|doi=10.1002/9780470034590|hdl=11693/53364|editor1-last=Harris|editor1-first=Robin K|editor2-last=Wasylishen|editor2-first=Roderick L|archive-date=2016-03-05|access-date=2015-03-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305131346/http://spin.niddk.nih.gov/clore/Pub/pdf/432.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bax pioneered the development of [[triple resonance experiments]] and technology for resonance assignment of isotopically enriched proteins.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Ikura M |author2= Kay LE |author3= Bax A |title=A novel approach for sequential assignment of 1H, 13C, and 15N spectra of proteins: heteronuclear triple-resonance three-dimensional NMR spectroscopy. Application to calmodulin. |journal=Biochemistry |volume=29 |issue=19 |pages=4659–67 |date=1990 |pmid=2372549 |doi=10.1021/bi00471a022}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=Lewis E Kay |author2=Mitsuhiko Ikura |author3=Rolf Tschudin, Ad Bax |title=Three-dimensional triple-resonance NMR spectroscopy of isotopically enriched proteins |journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance |volume=89 |issue=3 |pages=496–514 |date=1990 |doi=10.1016/0022-2364(90)90333-5|bibcode = 1990JMagR..89..496K }}</ref> Together with Torchia and [[Lewis E. Kay]], he developed the now widely adopted methods for studying atomic motions in proteins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kay |first1=Lewis E. |last2=Torchia |first2=Dennis A. |last3=Bax |first3=Ad |date=2002-05-01 |title=Backbone dynamics of proteins as studied by nitrogen-15 inverse detected heteronuclear NMR spectroscopy: application to staphylococcal nuclease |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/bi00449a003 |access-date=2025-03-03 |journal=Biochemistry |volume=28 |issue=23 |pages=8972–8979 |language=EN |doi=10.1021/bi00449a003|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Bax also pioneered the use of [[residual dipolar coupling]]s<ref>{{cite journal |author=Tjandra N |author2=Grzesiek S |author3= Bax A |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume= 118 |issue=26 |pages= 6264–6272 |date=1996 |title=Magnetic field dependence of nitrogen-proton J splittings in 15N-enriched human ubiquitin resulting from relaxation interference and residual dipolar coupling |doi=10.1021/ja960106n}}</ref> and [[chemical shift]]s<ref>{{cite book |author=Kontaxis G |author2=Delaglio F |author3= Bax A |chapter=Molecular Fragment Replacement Approach to Protein Structure Determination by Chemical Shift and Dipolar Homology Database Mining |title=Nuclear Magnetic Resonance of Biological Macromolecules |series=Methods in Enzymology |volume=394 |pages=42–78 |date=2005 |doi=10.1016/s0076-6879(05)94003-2|pmid=15808217 |isbn=9780121827991 }}</ref> for determining [[DNA]]<ref>{{cite journal |author= Boisbouvier A |author2= Delaglio F |author3 =Bax A |title=Direct observation of dipolar couplings between distant protons in weakly aligned nucleic acids |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=100 |issue= 20 |pages=11333–11338 |date=2003 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1534664100|bibcode = 2003PNAS..10011333B |pmid=12972645 |pmc=208757|doi-access= free }}</ref> and [[protein structure]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Bax A |author2=Grishaev A |title=Weak alignment NMR: a hawk-eyed view of biomolecular structure |journal=Curr. Opin. Struct. Biol. |volume=15 |issue=5 |pages=563–70 |date=October 2005|pmid=16140525 |doi=10.1016/j.sbi.2005.08.006 }}</ref>
Much of his recent work focuses on the use of rapid jumps in pressure inside the NMR sample cell to study mechanisms of protein folding and misfolding,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Charlier |first1=Cyril |last2=Alderson |first2=T. Reid |last3=Courtney |first3=Joseph M. |last4=Ying |first4=Jinfa |last5=Anfinrud |first5=Philip |last6=Bax |first6=Adriaan |date=2018 |title=Study of protein folding under native conditions by rapidly switching the hydrostatic pressure inside an NMR sample cell |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=115 |issue=18 |pages=E4169–E4178 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1803642115 |doi-access=free |pmc=5939115 |pmid=29666248|bibcode=2018PNAS..115E4169C }}</ref> the latter of potential importance to amyloid diseases.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=C. Ashley |last2=Robertson |first2=Angus J. |last3=Louis |first3=John M. |last4=Anfinrud |first4=Philip |last5=Bax |first5=Ad |date=2019-09-04 |title=Observation of β-Amyloid Peptide Oligomerization by Pressure-Jump NMR Spectroscopy |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=141 |issue=35 |pages=13762–13766 |doi=10.1021/jacs.9b06970 |issn=0002-7863 |pmc=9357264 |pmid=31432672|bibcode=2019JAChS.14113762B }}</ref> He was the world's most cited chemist over two decades (1981-1997).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://in-cites.com/nobel/2002-nobel-chemistry.html |title=Citation Laureates: Chemistry |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021102021041/http://in-cites.com/nobel/2002-nobel-chemistry.html |archive-date=2 November 2002 |work=In Cites |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://pcb4122.univ-lemans.fr/citation.html |title=50 Most Cited Chemists 1981-1997 |website=pcb4122.univ-lemans.fr |access-date=12 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030301122315/http://pcb4122.univ-lemans.fr/citation.html |archive-date=1 March 2003 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Work on human-generated aerosols ==
Using laser light scattering, Bax proposed that speech-generated aerosols are likely a dominant [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV-2]] transmission mode, demonstrating that speech aerosols remain airborne much longer than was widely believed hitherto.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Anfinrud|first1=Philip|last2=Stadnytskyi|first2=Valentyn|last3=Bax|first3=Christina E.|last4=Bax|first4=Adriaan|date=2020-05-21|title=Visualizing Speech-Generated Oral Fluid Droplets with Laser Light Scattering|journal=New England Journal of Medicine|volume=382|issue=21|pages=2061–2063|doi=10.1056/nejmc2007800|pmid=32294341|pmc=7179962|issn=0028-4793|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stadnytskyi|first1=Valentyn|last2=Bax|first2=Christina E.|last3=Bax|first3=Adriaan|last4=Anfinrud|first4=Philip|date=2020-06-02|title=The airborne lifetime of small speech droplets and their potential importance in SARS-CoV-2 transmission|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=117|issue=22|pages=11875–11877|doi=10.1073/pnas.2006874117|issn=0027-8424|pmc=7275719|pmid=32404416|bibcode=2020PNAS..11711875S |doi-access=free}}</ref> His group also developed novel technologies for capturing exhaled breath particles in a manner that enables quantitative chemical analysis of lung fluid by NMR and mass spectrometry.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kakeshpour |first1=Tayeb |last2=Louis |first2=John M. |last3=Walter |first3=Peter J. |last4=Bax |first4=Ad |date=2025-02-25 |title=Chemical Analysis of Deep-Lung Fluid Derived from Exhaled Breath Particles |journal=Analytical Chemistry |volume=97 |issue=7 |pages=4128–4136 |doi=10.1021/acs.analchem.4c06422 |issn=0003-2700 |pmc=11859745 |pmid=39949307|bibcode=2025AnaCh..97.4128K }}</ref>
